text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Parliament endorsed government proposal to create five large provinces in place of present 11 inland provinces. Parties were divided on the issue, and the vote in favour was close at 102-92.
- Finns get tax rebates paid into their accounts today.
- Two-thirds of Finns have a positive attitude towards part-time jobs, poll shows. @
- Finance Ministry official Kari Nars again Finland's candidate to join executive board of European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, where he served 1991-94.
- Finland's biggest literature award, the Finlandia prize worth 100,000 markka, went to little-known Helsinki writer Irja Rane for her book "Laughing Virgin."
- Helsinki's Museum of Foreign Art bought a painting by 18th-century Italian master Giambattista Tiepolo for small change. @
KAUPPALEHTI
- Asset arrangements between big Finnish forestry firms bring forest owners' cooperative Metsaliitto group into the eastern Finland wood market.
- Forest owners want forestry companies to publish price lists during future timber sales talks.
- Revised government proposal would allow Bank of Finland's parliamentary supervisors to participate in monetary policy decision-making for a few more years. @
- Personal computer sales a big factor in Finnish home appliance retail sector, where computer speciality shops have clear lead over conventional home appliance outlets.
- Beverage group Hartwall still negotiating for renewal of its Coca Cola distributers' licence.
AAMULEHTI
- Domestic violence kills 30 Finns every year, with more Finnish women likely to die at the hands of spouses than their American counterpaprt.
- Majority of Finns view part-time work in a positve light, and would prefer that to unemployment, poll shows. @
DEMARI
- Parliament approved revised energy tax bill, to raise households' electricity bills slightly in 1997.
- Tens of thousands of Finnish families trapped in circle of family violence but victims remain silent to keep up appearances, study presented at seminar shows.
